title: Protocol Mirror
pitch: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call.
about_excerpt: Did the trial publish what it registered? Protocol Mirror gives an AI agent WebMCP tools to trace the record, quote the evidence, and stage a proposal. A human makes the final call. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Protocol Mirror opens on a real ACTT-1 case with seven WebMCP tools ready for an agent-led, human-reviewed investigation. Original ClinicalTrials.gov outcomes sit beside PubMed evidence, with registry changes and exact source text visible. The responsive mobile view preserves the complete agent and reviewer workflow without horizontal scrolling. A 24-pair real-world stress test shows two local models making opposite errors from the same evidence. The session log separates every agent tool call from each human decision, creating a visible audit trail. An evidence-linked proposal remains in the review queue until a human accepts or rejects it. The evidence drawer places the agent’s reasoning beside exact quotations, source locators, and visible uncertainty. After a human decision, the eighth WebMCP tool appears and can export only the reviewed result. Inspiration I have a passionate affection for medicine. I also love using AI in my day-to-day life. I use it to learn new topics or subjects, research problems and examples, assist me in making cool apps such as my AI trading bot, and turn my brain dump of ideas into a working prototype. All of these use cases are reasons why I love AI. However, as I used AI more, one problem bothered me: AI, or an LLM, can give a fluent and confident answer even when the evidence behind it is incomplete or uncertain. In medicine and clinical research, we cannot afford to guess. Clinical trials are a good example of this. A trial registry records what researchers planned to measure, while a publication reports what readers eventually see. Comparing them requires searching through multiple registry pages and carefully matching the exact wording. This can be exhausting for a person and often takes a long time to complete. An AI agent could make the investigation faster and more efficient, but giving it the final judgment would create another problem. This problem inspired me to create Protocol Mirror: “Can an AI agent do the difficult, intensive investigative work while keeping the final decision in the hands of a human?” Protocol Mirror uses WebMCP to let an agent retrieve evidence, trace dated changes, quote exact source text, and propose a conclusion inside the webpage for the reviewer to see. The agent is useful, but it cannot approve or reject anything because that decision is left to the reviewer. What it does Protocol Mirror compares a clinical trial’s registered outcomes with what appears in its publication. The default example uses the real ACTT-1 trial, connecting its ClinicalTrials.gov record and registration history with its PubMed report. Using WebMCP, the agent can: Retrieve the live ClinicalTrials.gov record Retrieve the live PubMed abstract Examine the trial’s registration history Find the outcomes that were registered first Quote exact evidence with source locators Stage a matched, omitted, introduced, or uncertain proposal Request that a human review the proposal The page initially shows seven tools. None of them can accept or reject a proposal. That decision is made by the human reviewer after reviewing the information. Once the reviewer has made their decision, Protocol Mirror shows an eighth tool that lets the agent export a reviewed “receipt.” It includes only human-approved results, the evidence, source locations, and the audit history. If the reviewer undoes their decision, that tool is removed. A session log also records what the agent has called and what the reviewer has decided. If the reviewer rejects something, the application requires a reason and allows the reviewer to add notes, which are then returned to the agent. This lets the agent revise the proposal instead of allowing the review to be the end of the conversation. How I built it I used Codex as an AI engineering collaborator throughout the entire project. My first prompts involved introducing Codex to the hackathon, providing it with the official rules, judging criteria, and WebMCP documentation, connecting the Devpost plugin to Codex, and researching common hackathon project patterns. I first wanted to understand what WebMCP was and how it could change the structure of an experience instead of being used only as a decorative integration. After choosing clinical trials as the use case, I gave Codex a set of boundaries: Use real ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed records. Preserve what the trial registered first. Connect every proposal to exact quotations and source locations. Treat external research text as untrusted. Give the agent no accept or reject tool. Make the human decision change the available tool surface. Test with real cases and record model failures. Keep benchmark results separate from clinical claims. One prompt did not create this entire project. It took a lot of planning, analysis, and development for it to become what it is today. Once Codex understood the challenge and had the necessary context, I used it to help create a plan, build the live-data adapters, model the evidence, implement the review workflow, improve the backend and frontend interface, examine security risks, and create the benchmarks. I reviewed each stage to find weaknesses before continuing. Near the end, I used Claude Code and followed the same process. I gave it the necessary context and background, then asked it to critique my project and identify what I should fix. I used Claude for two reasons. First, I wanted a fresh set of eyes to inspect my codebase. Second, Fable 5.1 had been released, and its enhanced thinking, reasoning, and coding capabilities helped find and fix bugs. I built the application with Next.js, React, TypeScript, GSAP, and WebMCP. Validated server routes retrieve public records from ClinicalTrials.gov and PubMed. The application converts them into stable outcomes and evidence spans with exact URLs and locators. The tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to navigator.modelContext . Pair-bound tools are registered again when the active trial changes. The receipt tool exists only while reviewed work exists. Each tool has a closed input schema, bounded values, runtime validation, and an AbortSignal for cleanup. Read tools identify their output as read-only and untrusted. The application also checks outcome and evidence identifiers against the active case, preventing a proposal from citing an identifier that the reviewer cannot inspect. I repeatedly asked Codex to reassess the project against the rubric at every stage, turning each weakness into the next engineering task to fix. The final checks covered WebMCP conformance, linting, TypeScript, the production build, 75 automated tests, and browser automation of the complete seven-to-eight-tool workflow.
